los.contentMd:
# Introduction to Micro:bits

Welcome! We'll be running this workshop:

- **Paul Nolan** | Training Ray Intern
- **Sophie Hayes** | Emerging Technologies Intern

Over the course of the workshop you'll go from never having coded a micro:bit to driving a radio-controlled car you programmed yourself.

You will be using this Tutors course throughout the workshop. Work through each lab step by step using the arrows or the menu on the left. If you get stuck, ask! Everyone gets stuck when they're coding, even professional developers.

## What is a micro:bit?

The micro:bit is a pocket-sized, programmable computer designed by the BBC to teach young people about coding and how software controls hardware.

You program it in **MakeCode**, a free website where you build code from blocks that snap together like puzzle pieces. When you're ready, you can switch the same code over to **JavaScript** or **Python** and see what "real" code looks like.

## The plan

| Part | What you'll do |
|------|----------------|
| 1. Introduction | Meet the micro:bit, set up MakeCode, download your first program |
| 2. Coding Basics | Events, the LED screen, variables, if/else, loops and functions |
| 3. Radio Communication | Send messages between two micro:bits and build a tilt remote |
| 4. Robot Car | Code a joystick remote and a car, then add power-ups and race |

## Objectives

By the end of this workshop you will be able to:
- Make the micro:bit react to inputs like buttons, shaking and tilting
- Use variables, if/else statements, loops and functions
- Send commands from one micro:bit to another using radio
- Code a working remote-controlled car

![Smiley](img/smiley.png)

los.title: Meet the micro:bit
los.contentMd:
# Meet the micro:bit

Before writing any code, take a look at your micro:bit. Everything you program will use these parts.

## Front

| Part | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| **LED screen** | 25 red lights in a 5 x 5 grid. You can show icons, numbers, words and animations. It can also measure light level. |
| **Button A and Button B** | Inputs. You'll use these all the time, e.g. "when button A is pressed, do something". |
| **Touch logo** (gold logo at the top) | Works like a third button you touch instead of press. *(micro:bit V2 only)* |
| **Pins** (gold strip at the bottom) | Connect the micro:bit to other electronics, like the motors in your car. |

## Back

| Part | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| **Processor** | The "brain" that runs your code. It also contains a temperature sensor. |
| **Accelerometer** | Senses movement: shaking, tilting and which way up it is. |
| **Compass** | Senses which direction the micro:bit is facing. |
| **Radio and Bluetooth antenna** | Lets micro:bits talk to each other wirelessly. This is how your remote will control your car! |
| **Speaker and microphone** | Plays sounds and hears noise levels. *(micro:bit V2 only)* |
| **USB socket** | Connects to your laptop to load code and power the micro:bit. |
| **Battery socket** | Runs the micro:bit without a laptop. |

> **Inputs and outputs.** An *input* is information going **into** the micro:bit (a button press, a tilt, a radio message). An *output* is something the micro:bit **does** (lights up LEDs, plays a sound, turns a motor). Almost every program you write takes an input and decides on an output.

## Quick check

Look at your micro:bit and find:
1. Button A and button B
2. The USB socket
3. The radio antenna (hint: it's on the back, labelled "BLE antenna")
4. Does yours have a gold touch logo? If so, it's a **V2**.

los.title: Setting up Coding Environment
los.contentMd:
# Setting up Coding Environment

Go to the following website: [Microbit editor](https://makecode.microbit.org/)

Make a new project and name it anything you want.

![Make project](img/newproject.png)

An environment will open up like below.

![Coding environment](img/environment.png)

1. This is a **virtual Micro:bit**, you can interact with the buttons and it will show what would happen on a real Micro:bit with whatever code/instructions you provide it with.
2. This is your **toolbar**. This is where your blocks of code lie that you can use to create whatever you want!
3. This is your **workspace**. This is where you join your blocks of code together (like a puzzle piece) to build your program. In this example I'm showing a heart icon forever which is displayed on the virtual Micro:bit.

los.title: Connecting your Micro:bit to your laptop
los.contentMd:
# Connecting your Micro:bit to your laptop

To load our code onto the Micro:bit we will need to connect it to our laptop by USB and do a few steps to get everything working.

### 1. Plug in the Micro:bit
Plug in the Micro:bit to the USB port of your laptop and load up a new project on the Micro:bit editor.

### 2. Make some code
For example, I have a simple example below that shows different icons based on which button you press on the Micro:bit.
These are called **On Event blocks** -> an event is something that happens when a certain input occurs.

![Simple Code](img/SimpleExample.png)

**Note:** You may find the code works as the Micro:bit is connected to the laptop but to get it loaded on the Micro:bit without needing a cable we will need to download the code.

### 3. Download the code onto the Micro:bit
Once you have your code completed, click **Download** in the bottom left of the editor and save it on the Micro:bit. The Micro:bit will flash while it's transferring the data, `NOTE: The LED WILL FLASH TWICE, once the second flash of LED on the Micro:bit stops, you can remove the cable.`

#### Downloading the code
![Downloading Code](img/Download.png)

#### Download the .hex file onto the Micro:bit (WAIT UNTIL SECOND FLASH OF LED STOPS!)
![Downloading onto Micro:bit](img/microbitdownload.png)

los.title: Your First Program: Name Badge
los.contentMd:
# Your First Program: Name Badge

Time to write some real code! You're going to turn your micro:bit into a name badge.

## The blocks you need

All of these are in the **Basic** (blue) section of the toolbox:

| Block | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| **on start** | Runs the code inside it **once**, when the micro:bit switches on |
| **forever** | Runs the code inside it **over and over**, forever |
| **show string** | Scrolls text across the LEDs |
| **show icon** | Shows a picture (heart, smiley, etc.) |
| **pause (ms)** | Waits. 1000 ms = 1 second |

## Build it

1. Drag a **show string** block into the **forever** block and type your name.
2. Underneath it, add a **show icon** block and pick an icon you like.
3. Add a **pause** block and set it to **1000** ms.
4. Watch the virtual micro:bit on the left. Your name should scroll, then your icon should appear, over and over.
5. Click **Download** and copy it onto your real micro:bit.

Your finished code should look like this:

![Name badge](img/name-badge.png)

## Extra challenges

- Use **show leds** to draw your own picture, pixel by pixel.
- Show your age with **show number**.
- What happens if you move your code from **forever** into **on start**? Why?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**on start** only runs **once**, so your name scrolls a single time and then stops. **forever** keeps repeating it.

</details>

los.title: Events and the LED Screen
los.contentMd:
# Events & the LED Screen

Making the micro:bit react

## What is an event?

An **event** is something that happens: a button gets pressed, the micro:bit gets shaken, a radio message arrives.

An **on event block** waits for that thing to happen and then runs the code inside it. Until the event happens, the code inside does nothing.

You use events in real life all the time:
- **When** the alarm goes off **→** get up
- **When** the bell rings **→** go to your next class
- **When** your phone buzzes **→** check it

## Event blocks in MakeCode

Event blocks are the ones with no notch on top. They don't need to be inside anything else. Most are in the **Input** (pink) section:

| Block | Runs when... |
|-------|--------------|
| **on button A pressed** | Button A is pressed (you can change it to B or A+B) |
| **on shake** | The micro:bit is shaken (click the dropdown for tilt left, logo up, free fall and more) |
| **on logo pressed** | The gold logo is touched *(V2 only)* |
| **on loud sound** | It hears a loud noise *(V2 only)* |

**on start** and **forever** are special events too. One runs at power-on, the other runs constantly.

## The LED screen

The **Basic** section has blocks to control the 25 LEDs:

| Block | Example |
|-------|---------|
| **show icon** | A heart, smiley, skull, etc. |
| **show leds** | Draw your own picture by clicking the squares |
| **show number** | `7` |
| **show string** | `"Hello!"` (scrolls if it's longer than one letter) |
| **show arrow** | Points North, East, South, West... *(under Basic → more)* |
| **clear screen** | Turns all LEDs off |

The **Led** section lets you control single lights using **x** (column, 0 to 4, left to right) and **y** (row, 0 to 4, top to bottom):

| Block | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| **plot x 2 y 2** | Turns on the middle LED |
| **unplot x 2 y 2** | Turns it off |
| **toggle x 2 y 2** | Flips it on/off |

## Example

This program shows a different icon depending on which button you press:

![Simple Code](img/SimpleExample.png)

> **Tip:** You can switch between Blocks, JavaScript and Python at any time. They're three ways of writing the **same** program.

los.title: Variables
los.contentMd:
# Variables

Giving the micro:bit a memory

## What is a variable?

A variable is like a storage box with a name written on it. Inside the box, you keep a piece of information. It lets the micro:bit **remember** something and use it, or change it, later.

Think of a game's scoreboard: the **score** starts at 0 and goes up every time someone scores. The score is a variable.

Variables can hold different **types** of information:

| Type | Example | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| **Number** | `score = 0` | Can do maths with it |
| **String** (text) | `firstName = "Joe"` | Text goes inside quotation marks `""` |
| **Boolean** | `reverseMode = True` | Only ever `True` or `False` |

This is how a variable called *firstName* looks in MakeCode:

![Variable](img/variable.png)

## Variables in MakeCode

Open the **Variables** (red) section and click **Make a Variable...**. Give it a name that describes what it stores, like `score` or `speed`, not `x` or `thing`.

You'll then get these blocks:

| Block | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| **set score to 0** | Puts a value in the box (replacing what was there) |
| **change score by 1** | Adds to the value. Use `-1` to subtract. |
| **score** (round block) | Reads what's in the box, so you can show it or use it in a decision |

## Example: counter

![Counter example](img/counter-example.png)

1. **on start**: set `count` to 0
2. Every time **A** is pressed: add 1 to `count`, then show it

> **Why does the car need variables?** Your car remembers its **radio group**, and your power-up code uses a variable to remember whether a power-up is running. Without variables, the micro:bit would forget everything instantly.

los.title: If and Else
los.contentMd:
# If & Else

Making decisions

## True or false?

**If** and **else** let the micro:bit make a decision based on whether something is **true** or **false**. (True and false values are a data type called **booleans**.)

You do this all the time without thinking:

```
if it's raining:
    wear a rain coat
else:
    wear a t-shirt
```

BUT what if it's snowing? You can add an **else if**:

```
if it's raining:
    wear a rain coat
else if it's snowing:
    wear a winter coat
else:
    wear a t-shirt     # none of the above were true
```

The micro:bit checks each condition **from top to bottom** and runs the **first** one that's true. Everything below it is skipped.

## In MakeCode

The **if** blocks are in the **Logic** (teal) section. Click the **+** on an if block to add **else if** and **else** sections.

This example shows *A* on the LEDs if button A is pressed, *B* if button B is pressed, and so on:

![If and else example](img/ifandelse.png)

## Comparisons

A condition is usually a **comparison**. These are in **Logic** too:

| Comparison | Means | Example |
|------------|-------|---------|
| `=` | equal to | `roll = 6` |
| `≠` | not equal to | `message ≠ "stop"` |
| `<` | less than | `temperature < 10` |
| `>` | greater than | `speed > 100` |
| `≤` | less than or equal to | `light level ≤ 50` |
| `≥` | greater than or equal to | `joystick Y ≥ 800` |

## And, or, not

Sometimes one comparison isn't enough. You can combine them:

| Block | True when... | Example |
|-------|--------------|---------|
| **and** | **both** sides are true | it's Saturday **and** it's sunny → go to the beach |
| **or** | **at least one** side is true | it's raining **or** it's snowing → wear a coat |
| **not** | the condition is **false** | **not** button A pressed |

> **Sneak peek at the car:** your joystick remote decides which way to drive using exactly these blocks:
> ```
> if joystick Y ≥ 800:      send "F"   (forward)
> else if joystick Y ≤ 200: send "B"   (backwards)
> else if joystick X ≤ 200: send "L"   (left)
> else if joystick X ≥ 600: send "R"   (right)
> ```

los.contentMd:
## Exercises ### Exercise 1: Speed limit Go back to your **speed setting** from the Variables lab. Use **if** so that `speed` can never go below **0** or above **100**. ### Exercise 2: Dice roll **Warm-up:** when you **shake** the micro:bit, show a random number from 1 to 6. Hints: * **pick random** is in the **Math** section * **on shake** is in the **Input** section **Level up:** instead of a number, show the dice face using **show leds**. You'll need: 1. A variable `roll`, set to **pick random 1 to 6** 2. An **if / else if** for each number, each with its own **show leds** picture ### Exercise 3: Tilt detector The micro:bit's accelerometer measures tilt as a number. Find **acceleration (mg) x** in **Input → more**. 1. **Investigate:** in a **forever** block, **show number** for **acceleration x**. Hold the micro:bit flat, then tilt it left and right. Write down roughly what numbers you see. 2. **Build:** using **if / else if / else**: - Tilted left → show a **West** arrow - Tilted right → show an **East** arrow - Flat → show a small square (or clear the screen) This is the **same logic** your car remote will use with the joystick! ### Exercise 4 (challenge): Night light **light level** (in **Input**) is a number from 0 (dark) to 255 (bright). Show a moon when it's dark and a sun when it's bright. Test it by covering the LEDs with your hand.

Solution 2 (level up) ![Dice faces](img/dice-faces.png)

los.title: Loops
los.contentMd:
# Loops & Functions

Repeating yourself without repeating yourself

## Loops

A **loop** repeats code so you don't have to copy the same blocks over and over. Loops are in the **Loops** (green) section:

| Block | What it does | Use it for |
|-------|--------------|------------|
| **forever** | Repeats until the micro:bit is switched off | Constantly checking a sensor or joystick |
| **repeat 4 times** | Repeats an exact number of times | Flashing a light 3 times |
| **while ... do** | Repeats **as long as** a condition is true | "While button A is **not** pressed, beep" |
| **for index from 0 to 4** | Repeats, counting up in a variable called `index` | Lighting up a row of LEDs one by one |
| **every 500 ms** | Runs every so often, in the background | A blinking light that doesn't stop other code |

### Example: flash a heart 3 times

![Flash heart](img/flash-heart.png)

### Example: light up the top row, one LED at a time

![Light row](img/light-row.png)

`index` goes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, so the LEDs light up from left to right.

> **Watch out:** a **while** loop whose condition never becomes false runs **forever**, and nothing after it will ever run!

A **loop** repeats code so you don't have to copy the same blocks over and over. Loops are in the **Loops** (green) section:

| Block | What it does | Use it for |
|-------|--------------|------------|
| **forever** | Repeats until the micro:bit is switched off | Constantly checking a sensor or joystick |
| **repeat 4 times** | Repeats an exact number of times | Flashing a light 3 times |
| **while ... do** | Repeats **as long as** a condition is true | "While button A is **not** pressed, beep" |
| **for index from 0 to 4** | Repeats, counting up in a variable called `index` | Lighting up a row of LEDs one by one |
| **every 500 ms** | Runs every so often, in the background | A blinking light that doesn't stop other code |

### Example: flash a heart 3 times

![Flash heart](img/flash-heart.png)

### Example: light up the top row, one LED at a time

![Light row](img/light-row.png)

`index` goes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, so the LEDs light up from left to right.

> **Watch out:** a **while** loop whose condition never becomes false runs **forever**, and nothing after it will ever run!

los.title: Functions
los.contentMd:
# Functions

## What is a function?

A function is a **saved set of instructions** with a name. Instead of building the same code over and over, you build it once and then **call** it whenever you need it.

The example below is a function called *happy_Heart*. It does three things in order:
[Show heart icon] → [Show smiley face] → [Clear screen].

Every time you **call** this function, all three steps happen automatically.

![Happy Heart](img/happyheart.png)

## Making a function in MakeCode

Functions live under **Advanced → Functions** in the toolbox:

![Advanced bar](img/advancedbar.png)

1. Click **Make a Function...** and give it a name that says what it does, like `speedUp` or `celebrate`
2. Put your blocks inside the **function** block
3. Use the **call** block wherever you want it to run

> **Why does the car need functions?** The finished car has functions called `speedUp`, `slowDown` and `banana`, one for each power-up. The main code just says "call speedUp" without needing to know every step inside it. That keeps the code short and easy to read.

los.title: Exercises
los.contentMd:
## Exercises ### Exercise 1: Icon functions Make two functions, each showing a different icon. Call one when you press **A** and the other when you press **B**. ### Exercise 2: Race countdown Every race needs a start! When you press **A**: 1. Count down **3, 2, 1** on the screen (one second each) 2. Show **"GO!"** (or a big tick icon) 3. *(V2)* Play a sound from the **Music** section Put your countdown in a **function** called `countdown`. Use a loop if you can! ### Exercise 3: Alarm Using a **while** loop: while button **B** is **not** pressed, play a tone and flash the screen. Pressing B switches the alarm off. Hint: **not** is in **Logic**, and **button B is pressed** is in **Input**.
Solution 1 ![Solution 1](img/solution1.png)
Solution 2 ![Countdown](img/countdown.png) **3 − index** gives 3, 2, 1 as **index** counts 0, 1, 2.
Solution 3 ![Alarm](img/alarm.png) Press **A** to start the alarm and hold **B** to stop it.

los.title: Challenges
los.contentMd:
# Challenges

You now know the building blocks behind nearly every program: **events, variables, if/else, loops and functions**. Try one of these mini projects before moving on to radio. Each one uses several of those ideas together.

### Rock, Paper, Scissors
Shake to pick randomly between rock, paper and scissors, and show a picture for each. Play against the person next to you.
Tutorial: [makecode.microbit.org/projects/rock-paper-scissors](https://makecode.microbit.org/projects/rock-paper-scissors)

*Extra:* add a secret special move that only appears 1 time in 10.

### Reaction timer
Wait a random amount of time, then light up the screen. Press **A** as fast as you can. Show how many milliseconds you took. (Hint: **running time (ms)** is in **Input → more**.)

### Hot Potato
Pass the micro:bit around. A hidden timer counts down and whoever is holding it when it runs out loses!
Tutorial: [makecode.microbit.org/projects/hot-potato](https://makecode.microbit.org/projects/hot-potato)

### Make your own
Anything you like, as simple or as complex as you want. Have a look at [makecode.microbit.org/projects](https://makecode.microbit.org/projects) for ideas.

# Radio Communication

Get two micro:bits talking wirelessly, then build a tilt remote that sends real driving commands.

los.title: Radio Communication
los.contentMd: Radio Communication

los.title: Radio Communication
los.contentMd:
# Radio Communication

Getting micro:bits talking

## What is it?

Micro:bits can send messages to each other wirelessly using their built-in radio. That's what makes remote controls possible, and it's how your joystick will drive your car.

We use **radio groups** so that only certain micro:bits listen to each other. It's like pairing wireless headphones to your phone: your music doesn't play in the headphones of the person sitting next to you. Micro:bits only hear messages sent on **their own group number** (0 to 255).

**EVERY TEAM MUST USE A UNIQUE RADIO GROUP NUMBER.** If two teams pick the same number, your remote will drive their car too!

## Radio blocks

These are in the **Radio** (pink) section:

| Block | What it does |
|-------|--------------|
| **radio set group 1** | Picks the group number. Put this in **on start**. Sender and receiver **must match**. |
| **radio send string "F"** | Sends a piece of text |
| **radio send number 0** | Sends a number |
| **on radio received receivedString** | An **event** that runs when text arrives. `receivedString` is a variable holding the message. |
| **on radio received receivedNumber** | Same, but for numbers |

## Senders and receivers

- The **sender** sends a message when something happens, e.g. a button press.
- The **receiver** waits for messages and decides what to do with them, usually with **if / else if**.

In the example below, the sender sends a string or a number depending on which button is pressed. The receiver shows whatever it gets on its LEDs.

![Sender_and_Receiver](img/sender-receiver.png)

> **Agreeing on a code.** The sender and receiver have to agree on what each message means. For your car, the team uses this code:
>
> | Message | Meaning |
> |---------|---------|
> | `"F"` | Forward |
> | `"B"` | Backwards (reverse) |
> | `"L"` | Turn left |
> | `"R"` | Turn right |
> | `"stop"` | Stop |

los.title: Exercises
los.contentMd:
## Exercises Get into **pairs**. One micro:bit is the **sender** and the other is the **receiver**. Agree on your team's radio group number first! > **Testing without two micro:bits:** when your code uses radio, MakeCode shows **two** virtual micro:bits. Press buttons on one and watch the other react. ### Exercise 1: Send a message **Sender** * In **on start**, set the radio group * On button **A**, send the string `"hi"`. On button **B**, send the number `7`. **Receiver** * In **on start**, set the **same** radio group * When a string is received, show it on the LEDs * When a number is received, show it on the LEDs ### Exercise 2: Tilt remote Build a remote control **without a car** and use the receiver's LEDs to pretend to be the car. **Sender (the remote):** in a **forever** block, use the tilt logic from the If & Else lab: | Tilt | Send | |------|------| | Left (**acceleration x** < -300) | `"L"` | | Right (**acceleration x** > 300) | `"R"` | | Forward (**acceleration y** > 300) | `"F"` | | Back (**acceleration y** < -300) | `"B"` | | Flat | `"stop"` | **Receiver (the pretend car):** **on radio received receivedString**, use **if / else if** to show an arrow for each message (`"F"` → North, `"B"` → South, `"L"` → West, `"R"` → East) and clear the screen for `"stop"`. Hint: inside the received event, compare **receivedString = "F"** using the **=** block from **Logic**. If forward and back come out the wrong way round, swap the `<` and `>` for **y**. Testing and fixing is a normal part of coding!
Solution 2: Sender ![Tilt sender](img/tilt-sender.png)
Solution 2: Receiver ![Tilt receiver](img/tilt-receiver.png) Swap the **showArrow** blocks for motor blocks and this **is** your car code. That's the next topic!

# The Remote (Sender)

Setting up the joystick

The **remote is the sender micro:bit**. One person in your team codes the remote while the other codes the car (next lab). You'll test them together at the end.

Your remote is a micro:bit plugged into a **Joystick:bit** controller. It has an analog stick (the "rocker"), four coloured buttons, and the micro:bit's own **A** and **B** buttons on top.

![controller](img/controller.png)

### Step 1
Create a new project, e.g. **RC-Car-Remote**

![Step 1](img/step1.png)

### Step 2
The joystick blocks aren't built in, so you need to add them as an **extension**. Click **Extensions** at the bottom of the toolbox.

![Step 2](img/step2.png)

### Step 3
Search **"joystickbit"** and click on it. A new **Joystickbit** section will appear in your toolbox.

![Step 3](img/step3.png)

los.title: Controller Code
los.contentMd:
# Controller Code ## Step 1: On start In **on start**: * **radio set group** to your team's number. Every team needs a **UNIQUE** radio group, and the car must use the same one! * **initialise** the joystick (from the **Joystickbit** section) * **show icon**, so you can tell the remote is switched on and running ![initialisejoystick](img/initialisejoystick.png) ## Step 2: How the joystick works The **rocker value of X** and **rocker value of Y** blocks give you a number for the position of the stick, from roughly **0** to **1023**: | Stick position | X | Y | |----------------|---|---| | Centre (resting) | ~525 | ~506 | | Pushed **up** | ~525 | high (≥ 800) | | Pulled **down** | ~525 | low (≤ 200) | | Pushed **left** | low (≤ 200) | ~506 | | Pushed **right** | high (≥ 600) | ~506 | Every joystick is slightly different, so the centre won't be **exactly** 525/506. That's why we use **ranges** instead of exact numbers. Test yours with **show number** if you want to check. ## Step 3: Stop when the stick is centred In a **forever** block, first check whether the stick is resting in the middle. If it is, send `"stop"` so the car doesn't drive off on its own: ![analog-atrest](img/analog_atrest.png) The finished remote uses a slightly wider range for Y (**300 to 600**) so a little wobble won't make the car twitch. ## Step 4: Directions Underneath, still inside **forever**, add an **if / else if** chain. **Do forward/reverse first!** | If... | Send | |-------|------| | rocker Y ≤ 200 | `"B"` | | else if rocker Y ≥ 800 | `"F"` | | else if rocker X ≤ 200 | `"L"` | | else if rocker X ≥ 600 | `"R"` | | else if button **A** is pressed | `"stop"` (emergency stop!) | Example of the reverse condition: ![backwards](img/backwards-controller.png) ## Step 5: Test it Use the **Radio** lab's trick: flash a spare micro:bit with a receiver that shows an arrow for each message. Or wait until your teammate's car is ready!
Check your work: the finished remote Change the `10` to your team's radio group. ![Finished remote](img/finished-remote.png) Open it in MakeCode: [Finished remote project](https://makecode.microbit.org/96640-63492-24223-76730)
## Extra challenges * Use the coloured buttons on the Joystick:bit (look for the button blocks in the **Joystickbit** section) to send extra commands, like a horn or a spin move. Your teammate will need to add them to the car too! * Show an arrow on the remote's LEDs for the direction you're sending.

los.title: Car
los.contentMd:
# The Car (Receiver)

Setting up the car

The **car is the receiver micro:bit**. While your teammate codes the remote, you'll code the car to listen for messages and drive the motors.

The car is a **Kitronik :MOVE Motor** buggy. The micro:bit slots into the front and controls the two wheels: one motor on the left, one on the right.

### Step 1
Create a new project, e.g. **RC-Car**

![step1](img/step1.png)

### Step 2
Click **Extensions** at the bottom of the toolbox.

![step2](img/step2.png)

### Step 3
Search **"kitronik move motor"** and click on it. A new **MOVE Motor** section will appear in your toolbox.

![step3](img/step3.png)

## How does a car turn with only two motors?

There's no steering wheel! The car turns by running its wheels at **different speeds or directions**:

| Left wheel | Right wheel | Car does |
|------------|-------------|----------|
| Forward | Forward | Drives forward |
| Reverse | Reverse | Reverses |
| Slow / stopped | Forward | Turns left |
| Forward | Slow / stopped | Turns right |
| Forward | Reverse | Spins on the spot! |

The **move [Forward] at speed [80]** block handles this for you. Pick Forward, Reverse, Left or Right from the dropdown.

los.title: Coding the Car
los.contentMd:
# Coding the Car ## Step 1: On start * **radio set group** to the **same number as your remote** * *(Optional)* **show icon** so you know the car is on ## Step 2: Listen for commands Add an **on radio received receivedString** block from **Radio**. All your driving logic goes inside it. Using **if / else if**, compare `receivedString` to each command your remote sends: | If received... | Do this (MOVE Motor section) | |----------------|------------------------------| | `"F"` | move **Forward** at speed **80** | | `"B"` | move **Reverse** at speed **50** | | `"L"` | move **Left** at speed **80** | | `"R"` | move **Right** at speed **80** | | `"stop"` | **stop** | Check with your teammate: these letters must match **exactly** what the remote sends. `"stop"` and `"Stop"` are different strings! Feel free to change the speeds (0 to 100). Trial and error is key! Reverse is slower on purpose, because it's harder to control. ## Step 3: Download and drive! 1. Download the code onto the car's micro:bit 2. Switch the car on (and make sure it has batteries!) 3. Switch on your remote and drive
Check your work: the finished car Change the `10` to your team's radio group. ![Finished car](img/finished-car.png)

los.title: Troubleshooting
los.contentMd:
# Troubleshooting

Car not doing what you expect? Work through this list. Real engineers call this **debugging**.

| Problem | Things to check |
|---------|-----------------|
| Car doesn't move at all | Is the car switched on? Are the batteries charged? Did the code actually download (wait for the second flash)? |
| Car doesn't respond to the remote | Do the remote and car have the **same radio group**? Is the remote switched on (can you see its icon)? |
| Car responds to someone else's remote | Two teams have the same radio group. Pick a new, unique number for **both** your remote and car. |
| Car drives off on its own | Your remote isn't sending `"stop"` when the stick is centred. Check the at-rest ranges with **show number**. |
| Car goes the wrong direction | Check the letters match on both sides (`"F"` vs `"f"`). Check your X/Y numbers on the remote. |
| One direction never works | Remember **else if** checks top to bottom. Is an earlier condition always true and blocking it? |
| Car is too fast to control | Lower the speeds in the car code. |

> **Debugging tip:** add a **show string receivedString** block at the top of your car's radio received event. Now the car shows every message it gets, so you can see exactly what the remote is sending. Remove it once you've found the problem, because scrolling text slows the car's reactions down.

los.title: Power-ups
los.contentMd:
# Power-ups

Mario Kart, but real

Your car can drive. Now let's make racing more interesting! Each car has an **RFID reader** underneath, and there are **power-up cards** hidden around the track. Drive over one and something happens:

| Card | Power-up | What happens |
|------|----------|--------------|
| 🍄 Boost | `speedUp` | Happy face, full speed (100) for 2 seconds |
| 🍌 Banana | `banana` | Silly face, "uh-oh" sound, the car **spins out** for 2 seconds |
| 🐢 Slow | `slowDown` | Sad face, crawls along at half speed (50) for 2 seconds |

While a power-up is happening, **your remote stops working**. No steering out of a banana spin!

## What is RFID?

**RFID** (Radio Frequency IDentification) is the same technology as your bus card, a contactless payment card, or a shop's security tag. Each card has a tiny chip with a **unique ID number**. When the card comes close to a reader, the reader powers the chip using radio waves and reads its number.

The car's code knows which ID numbers belong to which power-up.

## Get the code

The RFID reader needs some extra low-level code to talk to it, so you'll start from a ready-made project rather than from scratch:

1. Open the [RFID car project](https://makecode.microbit.org/S97008-07416-41442-62980)
2. Click **Edit Code** to make your own copy
3. In **on start**, change the **radio set group** number to **your team's number**
4. Download it to your car's micro:bit

Your remote doesn't need to change at all. It sends the same `"F"`, `"B"`, `"L"`, `"R"` and `"stop"` messages as before.

> **Note:** the banana sound needs a **micro:bit V2** (the one with a speaker). On a V1 everything else still works.

los.title: How it Works
los.contentMd:
# How it Works

Open the project and find each part below. Notice that it uses **every** coding concept from the Coding Basics topic.

## Variables: remembering the cards

In **on start**, each card's ID number is stored in a variable:

![RFID cards](img/rfid-cards.png)

There are two cards for each power-up, so you can hide more of them around the track.

## Loops and if/else: checking for cards

A **forever** loop constantly asks the reader: *"is there a card?"* The ID it finds goes into `current_id` (or `-1` if there's no card). Then **if / else if** decides which power-up to trigger:

![RFID forever loop](img/rfid-forever.png)

The **or** block means *"if it's card 1 **or** card 2, speed up."*

## Functions: one per power-up

Each power-up is its own **function**, so the forever loop stays short and readable:

![speedUp function](img/rfid-speedup.png)

The **banana** function spins the car by running the left motor **forward** and the right motor **in reverse** at the same time.

## The `interrupt` variable: ignoring the remote

This is the clever part. `interrupt` works like a **flag**:
- `0` means "normal driving, listen to the remote"
- `1` means "a power-up is happening, ignore the remote"

The radio received event checks the flag **before** doing anything:

![Radio received with interrupt check](img/rfid-interrupt.png)

Without this, your remote would send `"stop"` a split second after you hit a banana and cancel the spin straight away. Programmers use flag variables like this all the time.

los.title: Make Your Own Power-ups
los.contentMd:
# Make Your Own Power-ups Now make the power-ups your own. Remember to **download and test after every change**. ### Level 1: Tweak it - Change how **long** each power-up lasts (the **pause** inside each function) - Change the **speeds**. Is a boost of 100 too much on your track? - Change the **icons**, or draw your own with **show leds** ### Level 2: Add effects - Add a sound to **speedUp** and **slowDown** (V2 only, **Music** section) - Make the boost **flash** the screen using a **repeat** loop instead of showing one icon - Make the banana spin go the **other** way ### Level 3: Invent a new power-up Change what one pair of cards does by writing a new **function** and calling it instead. Ideas: - **Reverse controls:** for 5 seconds, left becomes right and forward becomes backwards. *(Hint: you'll need another flag variable, and the radio event will need to check it.)* - **Wiggle:** zig-zag left and right a few times - **Shield:** a card that makes you immune to the next banana ### Level 4 (advanced): Register a new card Every card has a different ID, so a new card needs its number added to the code: 1. Add an **on button A pressed** event that does **show number** with **Try read ID** (from the **MFRC522** section) 2. Hold your new card against the reader and press **A**. Write down the long number that scrolls past. (If it shows -1, the card wasn't detected. Hold it closer and try again.) 3. Make a new variable, e.g. `card7`, set it to that number, and add it to an **if** in the forever loop
> **Race day tip:** before the race, label your car **and** your remote with your team's radio group number. Then nobody can mix them up!
